functions-classes.summary: Know how TypeScript types functions (signatures, overloads, `this`, void callbacks) and classes (modifiers, abstract members, initialisation order and constructor types), and where compile-time checks stop and runtime behaviour begins.
points: Function types need parameter names: `(n: number) => string`. Call signatures (`{ (n: number): string }`) also allow properties; construct signatures use `new (...) => T`.
A `() => void` callback type accepts functions that return anything, but a function declared `(): void` may not return a value.
Overloads are tried top to bottom and the first match wins. Callers never see the implementation signature, and a union argument needs a signature that accepts the whole union.
`private`, `protected`, `readonly` and `override` are compile-time only. `#private` fields are enforced by the JavaScript runtime and can be brand-checked with `#field in obj`.

With ES2022 targets (`useDefineForClassFields`), derived fields initialise right after `super()` and before parameter properties are assigned; redeclared fields reset base values unless you use `declare`.
`implements` only checks a class against an interface. It never adds members or contextually types method parameters.
Use the polymorphic `this` return type for fluent APIs, and `abstract new (...args: any[]) => T` when a function must accept abstract classes.
traps: Writing `(string) => number` declares a parameter named `string` of type `any`.
Marking callback parameters optional (`index?: number`) forces every implementer to handle `undefined` for no benefit.
Calling an overridable method from a base constructor runs the override before the subclass's fields are initialised.
